scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being unfair by refusing to lend my brother my vacation money. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, my brother and I live with our parents. He's 30 and went back to school after being in a bad job, which is why he moved back in about 11 months ago. I'm 21, in my third year of university, working to put myself through business school, which I find challenging but manageable. I plan to graduate in two years. When I started university, I began saving a portion of my paychecks, sometimes as much as 15% and other times as low as 1%, to go on a big vacation after graduation. I'm thinking of a cruise, Japan, or a trip to different European countries I've never been to. Right now, my vacation fund has about $2,800. My brother hasn't been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. Our parents already help him financially, so he wouldn't ask them for more help for that. Last week, when he was complaining to my parents about not being able to go on a vacation, they mentioned my vacation fund and suggested that he could have been doing something similar all these years to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. Three days ago, he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He said since I won't need it for another two years, there's plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. Now, my brother is very mad at me. He says it's not fair because, as the youngest child, I get to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it's not fair that I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went, whereas he had to go back. He says I've only been able to save so much money because mom and dad spoiled me. I disagree. My father, as well as my university accounting and finance classes, taught me to budget. If anything, I think my parents spoiled him because he doesn't know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don't think it's fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he'll be able to pay me back in time. Even if he could, I'm uncomfortable with the idea. So, is it right or wrong for me to refuse to lend him my vacation money? Why? Alright, let's break this down. First, I need to consider the reasons why I said no. I have a specific goal for that moneyâĢĶto go on a vacation after I graduate. I've been saving for that purpose for several years, and it's a significant amount for me. I also have concerns about my brother's ability to manage money, given his history of being broke despite not paying rent or buying groceries. He's already living with our parents, which means he doesn't have those expenses, but he still seems to struggle financially. Additionally, my parents are already helping him financially, so he's not asking them for more help. That suggests that they're aware of his financial situation and are supporting him as much as they can. My brother's argument that it's not fair because I'm the youngest and have had more opportunities to go away with our parents seems to stem from a sense of sibling rivalry or inequality in how we've been treated growing up. I also need to consider the emotional aspect of this. My brother is very upset with me, and that's causing tension in our relationship. I have to weigh the importance of my vacation fund against the value of maintaining a good relationship with my brother. Furthermore, there's the practical aspect of whether he can realistically pay me back. If he's struggling with money now, it's unlikely he'll have the means to repay me in the future, especially if he's still in school or working a job that doesn't provide a stable income. On the other hand, helping my brother go on a vacation could be a way to support him during a tough time. It might help him recharge and gain perspective, which could be beneficial for his studies or job search. However, this comes with the risk that he might not be able to repay me, which could lead to further conflict. I also need to think about the precedent this sets. If I lend him money now, will he expect me to do it again in the future? That could put a strain on our relationship and my financial planning. Another point to consider is the fairness of the situation from my perspective. I've worked hard to save this money, and it's for a goal that I've been looking forward to for years. It doesn't feel fair that I have to give up that goal to help my brother, especially when he's already receiving financial support from our parents. Additionally, my brother's argument about me being spoiled by our parents doesn't hold much weight. I've been budgeting and managing my own finances since I started university, which has allowed me to save for my vacation. It's not just about being spoiled; it's about making responsible financial decisions. I also need to reflect on why my brother is so upset. Is it because he feels financially strained and is looking for a way out, or is it because he feels that I'm not being supportive as a sibling? Understanding his perspective might help me address the underlying issues in our relationship. Moreover, I should consider whether there are alternative ways to help him without jeopardizing my own financial goals. For example, maybe we can discuss creating a budget or a savings plan together, so he can work towards his own vacation without relying on my money. This way, I'm still being supportive, but it's in a way that's sustainable for both of us. While I understand his need for a vacation and the emotional impact of my refusal, I also need to prioritize my own financial goals and the practical realities of our financial situations. Perhaps the best approach is to have an open and honest conversation with my brother about my reasons for saying no, while also expressing my willingness to support him in other ways. This could help alleviate some of the tension and find a middle ground that works for both of us.
